paper_title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Autoregressive (AR) large language models generate tokens sequentially, requiring a model forward pass for
each new token. Speculative decoding amortizes this cost by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple
tokens for parallel verification in a single target-model pass, while preserving the target model’s output
distribution [7, 16]. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation by predicting multiple draft
tokens simultaneously. For example, DFlash conditions a lightweight block-diffusion model on target-model
features to generate an entire proposal in a single draft pass [8].
sections.content: However, improving parallel draft predictions does not necessarily translate into higher throughput. Verification accepts draft tokens only up to the first rejection, so later correct predictions contribute to mean accepted tokens (MAT) only if the preceding prefix is accepted. Training should therefore account for this prefix dependence when allocating supervision to improve MAT. Higher MAT, in turn, improves throughput only when the additional accepted tokens compensate for increased draftverify latency. These challenges motivate jointly considering prefix dependence in training and the MATlatency trade-off at inference. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion-drafter training and deployment-time inference optimization (Figure 1). position-wise loss factorization guides supervision allocation to improve MAT, while throughput factorization guides inference configuration selection through the MATlatency trade-off. For training, correctly predicted token contributes to MAT only if the preceding prefix is accepted. Training shapes position-wise supervision; inference selection balances MAT against latency. Right: six-task mean speedup for the displayed configurations from Table 3; each method uses its matched AR baseline. motivates examining not only prediction loss, but also which positions receive supervision and how their losses are weighted. We therefore factorize each positions loss contribution into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss: whether the position receives supervision, how strongly it is weighted, and how its prediction loss is computed. Training interventions affecting different factors can be studied separately, while those affecting the same factor should be considered jointly to account for potential interactions. Guided by this view, we design recipe combining mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. Section 3.1 details the motivation and design of each component. For inference, we factorize throughput into MAT and latency contributions as = MAT/T , where is the latency of one draftverify round. Guided by this factorization, we identify three broadly applicable configuration dimensions for diffusion drafters: target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size. We assess their joint effects on MAT and latency to guide configuration selection. Our cost analysis and empirical measurements motivate full target conditioning with negligible incremental overhead, drafter depth selection that balances MAT gains against latency, and workload-aware inference block size selection without retraining through mixed-horizon training. Together, these policies guide the selection of high-throughput configurations for different models and concurrency settings. Section 3.2 details the analysis and selection procedure. Our key contributions are: We formulate position-wise loss factorization to guide diffusion drafter training, yielding recipe that combines mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to improve MAT without additional inference-time computation. We factorize throughput as the ratio of MAT to latency, guiding the joint selection of target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size for high-throughput configurations across workloads. We validate the training recipe and inference configuration selection across target models, benchmarks, and concurrency settings through end-to-end comparisons and ablation studies.

sections.title:
2.1 Speculative Decoding
In each speculative decoding round, a lightweight drafter proposes bs − 1 tokens conditioned on the verified
context, where bs is the inference block size. The target verifies them in one parallel forward pass, accepts
the consecutive prefix before the first rejection, and emits a replacement token at that position or a bonus
token after full acceptance. Appropriate acceptance and replacement rules preserve the target model’s output
distribution [7, 16].

The conditional acceptance probability ak and the prefix-survival probability S(k) are ak = Pr(N 1), S(k) = Pr(N k) = j= aj. Mean accepted tokens (MAT) per round is τ = 1 + E[N ] = 1 + bs1 k=1 S(k), (2.1) (2.2) where the additional one counts the target replacement or bonus token. The product in S(k) captures the prefix dependence: draft token can contribute to accepted length only if all preceding draft tokens are accepted.

sections.title:
2.2 Block-Diffusion Drafting
Block-diffusion language models generate text by unmasking tokens within a block using the available context.
When used as speculative drafters, they predict multiple future tokens jointly rather than generating a
proposal autoregressively. The target model then verifies the proposal as described in Section 2.1.
sections.content: We adopt DFlashs target-conditioned block-diffusion architecture [8], which predicts all masked positions in single forward pass. Its bs-position draft block contains the latest target-generated token followed by bs 1 mask tokens. To condition these predictions on the verified context, hidden states from selected layers of the frozen target model are concatenated and fused through lightweight linear projection: hctx = Wf [h(ℓ1); . . . ; h(ℓt)] + bf , Wf RHDtHT . (2.3) Here h(ℓi) RHT represents the same context token at target layer ℓi; HT and HD are the target and drafter hidden widths, hctx RHD is the fused feature, and bf RHD is the projection bias. The target remains frozen. Each drafter layer uses its own projections to map the fused features into cached keys and values reused across rounds. Block positions attend to this context and bidirectionally to one another.

sections.title:
3.1 Training Recipe Design
The prefix-survival relation in Eq. (2.1) shows that a correctly predicted token contributes to MAT only if the
preceding prefix is accepted. Improvements in token-level predictions therefore need not yield corresponding
gains in accepted length. This motivates examining how supervision is allocated across positions to better
align training with the MAT objective.
sections.content: 3.1.1 Position-Wise Loss Factorization We formalize this supervision allocation through position-wise loss factorization. During training, each block consists of visible anchor token and 1 subsequent target tokens, where denotes the training horizon. mask pattern specifies which future tokens within the block are masked for prediction and which are revealed as context. For each future position relative to the anchor, let Ik indicate whether it is included in the training loss: the position must lie within the training horizon and be masked for prediction. We factorize its loss contribution as Lk = Ik {z} inclusion w(k) {z } weighting ℓ(k m, L) } {z prediction loss . 3 (3.1) Here Ik determines whether position receives supervision, w(k) controls how strongly that positions loss is weighted, and ℓ(k m, L) specifies the prediction loss under mask pattern and loss function L. The factorization accommodates different loss functions L. In this work, we use token-level cross-entropy throughout and do not explore alternative loss functions. The training horizon and mask pattern may vary across updates. For fixed position k, π(k) = EB,m[Ik] measures how frequently it receives supervision. This exposes the position-dependent allocation of training signal induced by horizon and mask choices.

sections.title:
3.1.2 Factorization-Guided Training Strategies
We use the factorization to analyze training strategies in terms of the factors they affect. For each strategy,
we explain its motivation and its effects on supervision, then examine interactions among strategies to guide
their joint design.
sections.content: Figure 2 shows that DFlash, with training and inference block sizes both Mixed-horizon training. set to 16, accepts the entire draft proposal in 10.9% of verification rounds, suggesting potential for longer continuations. Since extending inference beyond the training horizon can reduce acceptance length [8], we increase both training and inference block sizes to 32. As shown in Figure 2, this extends accepted lengths beyond 16 tokens, but also increases the proportion of rounds accepting only 14 tokens, indicating more early rejections. This trade-off motivates mixed-horizon training, in which we use {8, 16, 24, 32} with equal frequency. By varying the inclusion frequency π(k) = E[Ik], this strategy emphasizes early positions while retaining longhorizon coverage. Varying also changes the block context and thus the prediction-loss term ℓ(k m, L). As shown in Figure 2, mixed-horizon training reduces early rejections relative to fixed-32 training while retaining continuations beyond 16 tokens at the same inference block size. Figure 2 Mixed horizons reduce early rejections relative to fixed-32 training. Accepted-length distributions for Qwen3-8B hidden-9t9d checkpoints trained for six epochs. Probabilities average dataset-normalized histograms equally over the six evaluation tasks. The legend specifies training horizon and inference block size bs; shading marks lengths 14 and beyond 16. Intra-block unmasking. Random masking patterns provide data augmentation for diffusion language models [25]. Revealing different subsets of tokens exposes the model to diverse prediction contexts beyond fully masked blocks. We apply intra-block unmasking by mixing fully masked and partially revealed training blocks. During training, we retain fully masked future blocks with fixed probability. For the remaining blocks, we sample masking ratio from Beta distribution and randomly reveal the complementary subset of future positions. Revealed positions contain the corresponding target tokens and provide context without contributing to the prediction loss. Unmasking changes Ik by excluding revealed positions from the loss, and ℓ(k m, L) by providing context for the remaining predictions. Acceptance-weighted loss. Position-dependent loss decay assigns larger weights to positions near the beginning of each draft block [8], but assigns the same weight to given position across training examples, regardless of how likely the preceding draft prefix is to be accepted. We introduce acceptance-weighted loss (AWL), which dynamically weights each positions loss based on the likelihood that verification reaches it. AWL acts on the weighting factor w(k) in Eq. (3.1), replacing fixed position-dependent weights with prefix-dependent acceptance weights. The cumulative product of these acceptance scores reflects the sequential nature of verification: the token at position can be accepted only if all preceding draft tokens are accepted. An earlier prediction with low acceptance score therefore reduces the weights of subsequent positions. Unlike fixed position decay, AWL dynamically allocates supervision according to the acceptance scores of the drafters predictions, linking the training weights directly to the verification rule. Early in training, the drafters limited predictive ability yields low acceptance scores, suppressing later-position gradients and concentrating supervision near the start of each block. As the drafter improves its predictions at earlier positions, the cumulative acceptance weights of later positions increase, progressively extending supervision to longer prefixes. This progression aligns optimization with the verification process, suppressing gradient contributions from later positions when their preceding prefixes are unlikely to be accepted. Joint design. The factorization guides not only the design of individual strategies, but also their combination. Mixed-horizon training and intra-block unmasking share the inclusion and prediction-loss factors, motivating joint evaluation. Although each improves MAT alone, combining intra-block unmasking with mixed horizons {4, 8, 16, 32} degrades performance  (Table 1)  . Unmasking short blocks may leave too few masked tokens, providing limited learning signal. We therefore use {8, 16, 24, 32} to reduce short-block exposure. The combination then outperforms either strategy alone, though its gains are not additive, consistent with overlapping effects on shared factors. sections.title:
3.2 Inference Configuration Selection
The training recipe in Section 3.1 improves MAT without introducing additional inference-time computation.
For inference, we factorize throughput into MAT and latency contributions, highlighting the need to jointly
assess their changes. This view guides our analysis of three configuration dimensions in diffusion drafters:
target-conditioning depth t, drafter depth d, and inference block size bs. Our configuration-selection objective
is
sections.content: (t, d, bs) = arg max t,d,bs τ (t, d, bs) (t, d, bs) , where τ is MAT (Eq. (2.2)), is the latency of one draftverify round [23], and the starred variables denote throughput-maximizing configuration. We analyze these three dimensions to guide inference configuration selection. Full target conditioning. Since the target model already computes hidden features at all layers, increasing only enlarges the input to the fusion projection in Eq. (2.3), without changing subsequent drafter computation. Our FLOPs analysis shows that, for Qwen3-8B at bs = 16 and MAT 7, increasing from 9 to 35 adds only 2.75% of the target projection and MLP FLOPs (Appendix A.4). Including attention matrix products and drafter computation in the total would further reduce this fraction. Figure 3(a) complements this analysis with controlled profiling at fixed MAT of 16: throughput varies by less than 1% across the tested conditioning depths, with 0.53% decrease from = 1 to = 35. This small measured cost motivates using all available target features under the tested execution conditions. Unimodality-guided drafter depth selection. Each candidate drafter depth requires training separate drafter, making an exhaustive depth sweep costly. We therefore seek to locate the throughput-maximizing depth efficiently. Our depth study reveals diminishing returns in MAT: additional drafter layers yield progressively smaller acceptance gains (Figure 3(b)). In contrast, each additional layer introduces the same computation. At fixed inference block size, round latency grows approximately linearly with depth, as supported by controlled profiling (Appendix A.5). Together, these observations suggest unimodal throughput curve under the MATlatency factorization. To formalize this, fix target conditioning and inference block size, and let τd and Td denote MAT and round latency at depth d, with throughput Gd = τd/Td and MAT increment = τd+1 τd. Assume diminishing MAT increments, d+1 d, and linear latency, Td = Tfix + Tlayer, where Tfix comprises target verification and the depth-independent parts of drafting, and Tlayer > 0 is the latency added by each drafter layer. Adding one layer then changes throughput by Gd+1 Gd = Rd Td(Td + Tlayer) , Rd = dTd Tlayerτd. Since Rd+1 Rd = (d+1 d)Td+1 0, once an additional layer no longer increases throughput, further 6 layers cannot increase it either: Gd is unimodal in (Appendix A.6). Unimodality thus allows the throughput peak at each fixed block size to be located efficiently, e.g., by binary search. Figure 5 shows the corresponding empirical trend: throughput rises and then falls with drafter depth, with small local fluctuations. The highest measured throughput occurs at = 6 for bs = 16, 24, 32, and at = 4 for bs = 8. Block-size selection without retraining. Mismatch between training and inference block sizes can reduce MAT, making configuration search costly if separate drafter is trained for each candidate inference block size. Mixed-horizon training (Section 3.1.2) addresses this limitation. Table 2 shows that drafter trained with mixed horizons achieves higher MAT than the fixed-32 model at every tested inference block size and remains close to the fixed-16 model at bs = 16. For each candidate drafter depth, the same mixed-horizon checkpoint supports evaluation across candidate inference block sizes, enabling joint selection of depth and block size without retraining for each block size.

sections.title:
4 Experimental Evaluation
We evaluate DScout from two complementary perspectives: how much it accelerates inference, and how its
training recipe and inference configuration selection contribute to these improvements.
sections.content: Benchmarks and baselines. We evaluate on GSM8K [10] and MATH-500 [12, 21] (Math), HumanEval [9], MBPP [5], and LiveCodeBench [13] (Code), and MT-Bench [30] (Chat). We compare with EAGLE-3 [20], DFlash [8], and PARD-2 [2]. Each method uses an autoregressive (AR) baseline matched in target model, hardware, runtime, sampling, and concurrency. Training and implementation. We disable thinking mode for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. We train DScout, DFlash, EAGLE-3, and PARD-2 on the same 1.4M Open-PerfectBlend [15] examples with target-generated responses, following each baselines official training recipe. DScout follows DFlashs parameters [8], except Qwen3-8B uses our selected 35t6d configuration (Section 4.2). Training GPUs have 80 GB HBM and 3.35 TB/s bandwidth; main and serving benchmark GPUs have 192 GB HBM3 and 8 TB/s bandwidth. DScout, DFlash, and EAGLE-3 use SGLang [31] with FlashInfer [29]; PARD-2 uses its official Transformers runtime with separate matched AR baseline. Training settings and study protocols appear in Table 6 and Section A. Metrics and configuration selection. All evaluations are repeated five times. Speedup is the ratio of mean output throughput to matched mean AR throughput, computed per dataset and then averaged equally across datasets. Study-specific aggregation procedures are detailed in Appendix A. MAT (τ ) is defined in Eq. (2.2). At concurrency above one, throughput measures aggregate service output. We report both bs = 16 and bs = 32 for DScout.

sections.title:
4.1 End-to-End Performance.
Benchmark performance. DScout improves mean speedup over DFlash on both Qwen3 targets and at
both temperatures, reaching up to 4.14× over AR and about 9% over DFlash (Table 3). Longer proposals
help when their additional accepted tokens offset the extra draft–verify cost. On Qwen3-8B at temperature
0, this trade-off favors bs = 32 on the Math tasks, but bs = 16 on MBPP, LiveCodeBench, and MT-Bench,
where acceptance gains are smaller. The preferred block size also changes with temperature on Qwen3-4B.
Thus, drafting quality varies by workload, and higher MAT alone does not determine the fastest configuration.

sections.title:
4.2 Design Analysis
Training-recipe ablation. Following Section 3.1, we progressively add mixed-horizon training, intra-block
unmasking, and AWL to the training recipe. Each configuration is trained independently to produce a
separate checkpoint. At a common inference block size of bs = 16, the cumulative training ablation improves
MAT by 16.1% (Figure 4). Every added strategy contributes, with AWL producing the largest increment
after mixed horizons and intra-block unmasking. These gains require no additional inference-time operations;
the increments are conditional on the preceding recipe rather than independent effects. The system-level
comparison in Appendix Figure 7 shows higher acceptance at every position, with larger gains later in the
block.
sections.content: Drafter-depth selection. Figure 5 shows throughput increasing and then declining with drafter depth, with small local fluctuations. The highest measured throughput occurs at = 6 for bs = 16, 24, 32, but at = 4 for bs = 8, showing that the preferred depth depends on inference block size. The unimodality result applies under its stated assumptions; local measurement fluctuations need not satisfy it exactly. Together with the target-conditioning analysis in Section 3.2, these results motivate our 35t6d configuration for Qwen3-8B, with inference block size selected for each concurrency setting. 8 Table 4 Serving speedup and MAT across target models and concurrency levels at temp = 0.

sections.title:
5 Related Work
Autoregressive and parallel drafters. Early speculative decoding methods generate proposals autore-
gressively [7, 16]. The EAGLE family uses target-model features for drafting, with EAGLE-3 combining
multi-layer features and direct token prediction [18–20]. Other approaches reduce sequential drafting through
multiple prediction heads, as in Medusa and Hydra [3, 6], or parallel masked-token prediction, as in PARD [1].
sections.content: Block-diffusion drafters. Diffusion language models support parallel token prediction [4, 26] and have been explored for speculative drafting in DiffuSpec, SpecDiff-2, and DART [17, 22, 28]. DFlash generates proposals in single pass using target-conditioned block-diffusion drafter [8]. Building on this architecture, DScout studies how training supervision and inference configuration together determine decoding efficiency. Its two factorizations guide supervision toward accepted prefixes and configuration selection according to the MATlatency trade-off. Serving efficiency and inference configuration. vLLM and SGLang improve serving efficiency through memory management and scheduling [14, 31], while SpecInfer supports efficient token-tree verification [24]. Complementary to these systems, DScout selects target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size based on their MATlatency trade-offs. Mixed-horizon training further allows inference block size 9 to be selected for different workloads and concurrency settings without retraining the checkpoint.

sections.title:
6 Discussion and Conclusion
Our current inference selection uses a shared block size for each target model and concurrency setting.
A natural next step is to adapt block size online as acceptance and serving load change. Mixed-horizon
checkpoints support this flexibility without retraining. An online policy could use recent acceptance statistics
and measured round latency to adjust block size within a generation according to the MAT–latency trade-
off. Evaluating such a policy under changing workloads, while accounting for adaptation overhead, would
establish whether it yields sustained gains over fixed configurations.
sections.content: Overall, DScout provides systematic approach to translating diffusion-drafter prediction quality into practical decoding acceleration. For training, position-wise loss factorization guides strategy design and combination. For inference, the MATlatency factorization guides configuration selection. The resulting training recipe and inference configurations improve end-to-end performance across models, tasks, and serving loads. These factorizations can also inform future diffusion-drafter research by providing framework for training strategy design and inference configuration selection.

sections.title: A Evaluation Details and Supplementary Results
sections.content: A.1 Additional Setup and Aggregation Evaluation protocol. We use the six evaluation tasks defined in Section 4, with 128 prompts per task except MT-Bench (80), dataset seed 0, an 8192-token context limit, and 2048-token generation cap. Sampling uses top-p = 1, with top-k = 1 at temperature 0 and no top-k truncation at temperature 1; the corresponding sampling seeds are 1000 and 2000. SGLang runs use 32 warm-up prompts; PARD-2 uses one. DScout, DFlash and EAGLE-3 are trained for six epochs, and PARD-2 for two. These are complete-system comparisons with unequal training budgets. Each comparison uses its matched AR baseline; speedups across the SGLang and PARD-2 runtimes do not establish an absolute throughput ranking. Training-control studies and system benchmarks use separate platforms, and their latencies are not pooled. Run variability. Point estimates follow the task-level ratio-of-means definition in Section 4. For repeat variability, we instead compute one macro speedup per repeat by pairing candidate and AR runs with the same repeat index, then report the sample SD over five repeats. This measures variability on fixed prompts, not uncertainty over unseen tasks. Mechanism studies with different aggregation are specified below. A.2 Serving Configuration Grid We evaluate bs {8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 24, 32} for each target and concurrency setting. Figure 6 records every block-size candidate underlying DScout (best) in Table 4. Each targetconcurrency setting keeps its checkpoint fixed and selects one block size by maximizing equal-weight mean speedup across all six tasks. Thus, these results evaluate block-size selection at fixed (t, d), not joint optimum over all three dimensions. Selection uses the evaluation tasks themselves, without combining per-task optima. Table 5 reports repeat variability; entries are DFlash / DScout (best). 13 Figure 6 Full serving grid. Cells show six-task mean speedup; bold entries mark the selected block size in each row. The training-horizon controls use Qwen3-8B hidden-9t9d checkpoints trained for six epochs. Fixed-16 uses positional decay γ = 7; fixed-32 and mixed horizons use γ = 15. Mixed horizons sample {8, 16, 24, 32} equally. The distribution in Figure 2 averages dataset-normalized histograms over the same six tasks as the system benchmarks. Position-wise acceptance. Figure 7 compares final DScout (35t6d) with DFlash on Qwen3-8B. Let S(k) be the probability that the first draft tokens survive verification, with S(0) = 1. We compute conditional acceptance as S(k)/S(k 1) from each datasets accepted-length histogram in each run, then average equally over five repeats and datasets within each domain. Conditioning on surviving prefixes means these probabilities need not decrease with position. The comparison evaluates complete systems and does not isolate architecture, training-recipe, or training-budget effects. Drafter depth. Figure 3(b) and Figure 5 use the Qwen3-8B 35t hidden-conditioned family trained for six epochs, with = 1, {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12}, and bs {8, 16, 24, 32}. For each dataset, we discard the minimum and maximum of five repeats and average the middle three, then average equally across the six datasets. Figure 5 reports throughput in tokens per second (TPS); repeat-level dispersion is unavailable for these aggregates, so no error bars are shown. Highlighted maxima identify the best measured candidates, without implying statistically significant differences. 14 Figure 7 Position-wise conditional acceptance of DScout (35t6d) and DFlash at bs = 16, = 8, and temperature 0. A.4 Target-Conditioning Cost Measured throughput. Figure 3(a) sweeps = 1, . . . , 35 at fixed = 6, bs = 16, and = 1, with five repeats per setting. Acceptance is held fixed at 16 tokens per round to isolate execution cost from prediction quality. Let q(t) be trimmed-mean throughput and s(t) the across-repeat SD. Points show 100[q(t)/q(1) 1], and bars show 100s(t)/q(1) percentage points. The reference mean is fixed, so the bars represent run variability rather than confidence intervals for the ratio. These measurements capture end-to-end throughput, not isolated feature-fusion latency. Illustrative arithmetic cost. For concatenation followed by linear projection, increasing conditioning from 9 to 35 layers adds Ffusion = 2(35 9)H 2A, Ftarget,dense = 2LT bs (2H 2 + 2HK + 3HI), where is the number of newly fused context tokens and multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. The target term counts target projection and MLP FLOPs. Here LT is the target layer count, is the MLP intermediate width, and is the total key/value projection width. We use HT = HD = for equal target and drafter hidden widths. Using Qwen3-8Bs LT = 36, = 4096, = 12288, and = 1024,1 with bs = 16 and 7 corresponding to MAT near seven when only newly accepted context tokens are fused, these costs are 6.11 and 222.26 GFLOPs, respectively (2.75%); fusing all 16 positions gives 6.28%. This cached-context calculation excludes prefill, attention matrix products, the output head, drafter operations, and memory traffic. It illustrates arithmetic scale, not measured fusion profile or bound on latency; feature transfer and kernel behavior remain relevant. A.5 Controlled DepthLatency Profiling To examine execution cost independently of prediction quality, we profile drafter depths = 1, . . . , 35 with fixed acceptance length. Let qd denote the measured throughput. Under this fixed-acceptance protocol, relative round latency is Td/T1 = q1/qd. Figure 8 plots this ratio with an unconstrained least-squares affine fit, Td/T1 0.9777+0.0190d, yielding R2 = 0.9975. The maximum relative deviation from the fitted line is 1.86%. These measurements support approximately linear latency over the profiled depth range, complementing the MAT increments and end-to-end throughput in Figure 3(b) and Figure 5. 1Model dimensions: Qwen3-8B configuration. 15 Figure 8 Depthlatency profile. Measured relative round latency and affine fit. A.6 Conditional Unimodality over Drafter Depth Fix target conditioning, inference block size, workload, and execution conditions. On finite interval of consecutive drafter depths, let τd > 0 be MAT, Td > 0 be mean round latency, and = τd+1 τd. Write the per-layer latency increment as bd = Td+1 Td > 0. Assume diminishing MAT increments, d+1 d, and non-decreasing latency increments, bd+1 bd. Then throughput Gd = τd/Td is unimodal in the sense that it is non-decreasing up to some depth and non-increasing thereafter (equivalently, quasi-concave in d): its increments cannot become positive after becoming nonpositive. Plateaus and boundary optima are permitted; MAT need not be monotonically increasing. The linear latency model in the main text is the special case bd = Tlayer. Proof. Since Td > 0 and Td+1 > 0, Gd+1 Gd = Rd TdTd+1 , Rd = dTd bdτd, so the sign of each throughput increment is the sign of Rd. Using τd+1 = τd + and Td+1 = Td + bd gives Rd+1 Rd = (d+1 d)Td+1 (bd+1 bd)τd+1 0, where the first term is nonpositive by diminishing MAT increments and the second is nonpositive because latency increments do not decrease and τd+1 > 0. Thus Rd is non-increasing, and once Rd 0, every subsequent throughput increment is nonpositive. This proves the claim. Under linear latency, the second term vanishes, so the sign change is driven by the diminishing MAT increments alone. Relation to the measurements. Figure 3(b) motivates diminishing returns over the consecutive measured depths 28. Its final row reports the total gain from depth 8 to 12, not one-layer increment, and does not resolve the unmeasured intermediate depths. Figure 5 shows throughput rising and then falling with small local fluctuations; it does not by itself establish exact unimodality. The separate fixed-acceptance profile in Appendix A.5 supports approximately linear latency. The proposition provides search rationale under It applies explicit assumptions, rather than an unconditional guarantee for the measured serving curves. separately at each fixed block size: it does not establish unimodality of the envelope maxbs G(d, bs) or global optimum over all configurations.
